security_audit.summary: The static Ruby backtick and hardcoded URL findings are false positives caused by Markdown examples and public reference links. No prompt injection or malicious exfiltration intent was found. A separate medium semantic risk remains because several documented Git commands can remove local work if an agent runs them without explicit confirmation.

remediation.issue: Destructive Git commands can remove local work or rewrite history.
remediation.suggestion: Require status checks, backups, and explicit user confirmation before reset hard, force delete, stash clear, remote delete, or force push commands.

remediation.issue: Remote Git operations are shown as direct commands.
remediation.suggestion: Tell agents to confirm remote names, branches, and URLs before push, pull, fetch, delete, or force-with-lease operations.

remediation.issue: Global Git configuration examples change developer-wide settings.
remediation.suggestion: Add guidance to prefer repository-local configuration when the change is only needed for one project.

semantic_findings.title: Destructive Git Commands Need Explicit Confirmation
semantic_findings.description: The guide includes destructive Git operations such as force branch deletion, stash clearing, and hard reset. Without mandatory confirmation and backup checks, an agent could remove local work when applying the workflow.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited sections show destructive Git operations with only limited caution text. These commands have legitimate recovery uses, so the risk is data-loss focused rather than clearly malicious.

content.user_title: Manage Git Workflows With Safer Branching
content.value_statement: Git work can become slow or risky when branches, commits, and conflicts are handled inconsistently. This skill gives structured Git workflows for branching, committing, merging, rebasing, and cleanup.
actual_capabilities: Explains branch creation patterns and branch naming conventions.
Guides staging, status checks, diffs, and focused commits.
Provides Conventional Commit message structure and examples.
Covers push, pull, fetch, merge, and rebase workflows.
Outlines conflict resolution steps for merge and rebase cases.
Includes cleanup, stash, cherry-pick, bisect, history, and configuration guidance.
limitations: It does not inspect a repository unless the host agent runs Git commands.
Several commands can rewrite history or remove local work if used incorrectly.
It assumes Git is installed and repository remotes are already configured.
It does not replace team review, release, or testing policies.

use_cases.title: Ship a Feature Branch
use_cases.description: Plan a clean branch workflow from latest main through commits, push, review, merge, and cleanup.

use_cases.title: Handle Release Fixes
use_cases.description: Use a focused hotfix flow with clear commits, remote updates, and post-merge cleanup.

use_cases.title: Resolve Collaboration Conflicts
use_cases.description: Follow repeatable merge or rebase steps when teammates change the same files.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Branch Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me create a Git branch workflow for a new feature. Include branch naming, status checks, commit guidance, push steps, and cleanup.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare Commit Messages
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my intended changes and suggest focused Conventional Commit messages. Separate unrelated work into different commits.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve a Conflict
prompt_templates.prompt: Guide me through resolving a Git conflict. Ask for the current status, identify conflicted files, and explain safe next steps.

prompt_templates.title: Plan History Cleanup
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me clean up recent Git history before review. Explain rebase, squash, amend, and recovery options, and ask before destructive commands.

output_examples.input: I need to start work on a user profile feature.
output_examples.output: A short branch workflow with status review, branch naming, focused commits, remote push, pull request review, and branch cleanup.

output_examples.input: My rebase stopped because two files conflict.
output_examples.output: A conflict checklist that identifies conflicted files, explains marker review, stages resolved files, and continues or aborts safely.

output_examples.input: I changed authentication tests and profile documentation.
output_examples.output: A recommendation to split the work into separate focused commits with clear Conventional Commit subjects.

best_practices: Check status and diffs before staging, committing, rebasing, or deleting branches.
Ask for explicit confirmation before force push, reset, stash clear, or branch deletion.
Keep commits focused and write messages that explain both what changed and why.
anti_patterns: Running destructive Git commands without confirming the current branch and uncommitted work.
Committing generated files, secrets, or unrelated changes with feature work.
Rebasing or rewriting shared branch history without team agreement.

faq.question: Can this skill run Git commands automatically?
faq.answer: The skill provides Git workflow guidance. Command execution depends on the host tool permissions and user approval.

faq.question: Does it support both merge and rebase workflows?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains merge, no fast-forward merge, rebase, continue, and abort flows.

faq.question: Can it help with merge conflicts?
faq.answer: Yes. It outlines how to identify conflicted files, resolve markers, stage changes, and continue the workflow.

faq.question: Does it create pull requests?
faq.answer: No. It describes the surrounding Git workflow, but it does not automate pull request creation.

faq.question: Is it safe for production hotfixes?
faq.answer: It can guide hotfix steps, but teams should still follow release checks, reviews, and tests.

faq.question: Can it recover lost work?
faq.answer: It includes recovery concepts such as reflog and branch recreation, but recovery success depends on repository state.
